title: Laws of Attraction
full_review:
Can two bickering divorce attorneys find marital bliss after they wake up wedded? "Laws of Attraction" (New Line) poses this question in a visually appealing but underwhelming romantic comedy. It's got a good message about commitment but it lags on laughs.

Audrey (Julianne Moore) is a high-powered New York City attorney unfettered by romantic relationships, much to the regret of her Botox-happy, ex-model mom (a frisky Frances Fisher) who is content to pass as Audrey's sister.

Fiercely competitive in the courtroom, Audrey meets her match when disheveled Daniel (Pierce Brosnan) returns to the Big Apple. He's a by-the-seat-of-his-pants type guy who always gets juicy divorce settlements for his clients.

In court he and Audrey are steely rivals. But Daniel, a romantic at heart, finds her fascinating and over dinner and far too many drinks his charm melts her defenses. To bed they go -- and to court the next morning. When he uses a down 'n' dirty tactic to win, all hope for a relationship seems doomed.

Enter a splitsville couple: rock star Thorne (Michael Sheen) and his funky designer wife, Serena (Parker Posey). Daniel represents her while Audrey has the philandering husband. And both spouses want sole possession of only one thing: their castle in Ireland.

Before you can spell "leprechaun," each attorney has winged it to the Emerald Isle to gather favorable testimony from the castle staff. Once again, Audrey and Daniel imbibe a little too much of the local brew and wake up together dressed in wedding rings and with murky memories of a priest marrying them the night before.

He's pleased; she's not. Upon returning to New York, where their marriage has already hit the gossip columns, they decide they'd better keep up a marital front while cohabiting platonically.

On the plus side, the movie is undeniable eye candy, with a gorgeous-to-look-at cast. Brosnan plays it low-key dashing, and Moore is at the height of her beauty, shedding crystalline tears reminiscent of another Moore -- Demi -- in "Ghost."

Yet you are always aware that these two are acting with a capital A. They have been far better in other roles, as has the often-remarkable Posey. She is considered queen of the indie films, but in this big Hollywood film she barely registers.

Clearly, the movie is a throwback to 1940s screwball comedies, but without the wit the snappy comebacks are few and far between.

Compensating somewhat for this is a sumptuous production design, from tony apartment interiors to softly rolling Irish hillsides. Visual panache it's got in droves, but the script doesn't always make sense of the characters' actions. At least it all comes down on accepting that marriage requires commitment and work, not to be discarded at the first hint of discontent.

Seventeen individuals are listed as producers in the credits; perhaps movie-by-committee is why this ended up as escapist forgettable fare. For a similarly themed but truly fine example of screwball comedy at its best, look at Katharine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy in 1949's "Adam's Rib."

Due to implied sexual encounters following inebriation, impersonation of a cleric, a few crude expressions and an instance of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
